classification.difficultyReason: Translate teenage ages into allowable prime-factor groups and use exclusive prime factors followed by remaining exponent counts to determine every age multiplicity.

content.prompt: A teacher multiplied the ages of all of the students (all teenagers) in her class and came up with the number $15\,231\,236\,267\,520$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the prime factorisation of this number?

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use the prime factorisation to help you work out the number of students in the class, their ages and the number of students of each age.

inlines.text: 11 students: one aged 13, three aged 14, one aged 15, one aged 16, two aged 17, two aged 18 and one aged 19.
Group all prime factors into ages from 13 to 19, using each factor exactly as often as it occurs.

answer.worked:
The possible whole-number teenage ages are 13 to 19. Their prime factors are:
$$13,\quad14=2\times7,\quad15=3\times5,\quad16=2^4,\quad17,\quad18=2\times3^2,\quad19.$$
The factors $13$, $17^2$ and $19$ give one student aged 13, two aged 17 and one aged 19. Only age 14 contains a factor of 7, so $7^3$ gives three students aged 14. Only age 15 contains a factor of 5, so there is one student aged 15.
These three 14-year-olds use $2^3$, and the 15-year-old uses one factor of 3. The remaining factors are $2^6\times3^4$. The four remaining factors of 3 require two 18-year-olds, using $2^2\times3^4$. The remaining $2^4$ gives one 16-year-old.
Thus the age counts are $13:1$, $14:3$, $15:1$, $16:1$, $17:2$, $18:2$, $19:1$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Number of students}&=1+3+1+1+2+2+1\\\text{Number of students}&=11.\end{align*}$$
